title: Fractions, percentages and proportional comparisons
transcript: A percentage is a fraction with denominator one hundred. A fraction, a decimal and a percentage can describe the same share. Give every percentage a base amount. If the base changes, the absolute size of the same percent changes too.

In AMC practice, percentages may compare scores, discounts or part of a collection. Convert to one form to make fair comparisons. A Rossmoyne style problem may apply two percentage changes. Keep the base for each change and work with exact multipliers.
Find twenty-five percent of one hundred and twenty-four. Write the percent as an exact fraction before multiplying. Can you simplify the fraction to make each part easier to find?

twenty-five percent means twenty-five over one hundred. Its simplified form is one over four. Take this fraction of one hundred and twenty-four. The result is thirty-one. It is smaller than the original because the percent is below one hundred.

Team A answers eighteen out of forty-five correctly. Team B answers fifty-six out of one hundred and twenty-five correctly. Which accuracy is higher? Compare the fractions, since the teams faced different numbers of questions.

Express the shares over a common denominator, or compare the cross products. Multiply eighteen by one hundred and twenty-five for A. For B multiply fifty-six by forty-five. Compare the numerators over the same positive denominator. Team B has the higher accuracy. It has the larger numerator after a fair comparison. The totals of correct answers alone were not enough.

A price is increased by twenty percent. The new price is then reduced by twenty-five percent. The final price is three hundred and sixty dollars. What was the original price? Each percent acts on the price immediately before that change.

The discount leaves seventy-five percent of the increased price. Undo it by dividing the final price by three over four. The increased price was four hundred and eighty dollars. It is one hundred and twenty percent of the original. Divide again to undo that increase. The original price was four hundred dollars. Check by applying the increase first and taking the discount from that result.

The combined multiplier is six over five times three over four, which is nine over ten. Multiplying the original price by that factor returns the final price. Subtracting the two percentage numbers would use the same base for both changes.

Compare proportions with a common denominator. A larger numerator by itself says little when the totals differ. A price reduction of twenty percent leaves eighty percent. Use the amount that remains as a multiplier.

Name the base under every percentage. Convert to a fraction or a multiplier you can check exactly. When several percentages act in sequence, write one multiplier for each step. Reverse division and multiplication in the correct order.
